newsitem.title: CANADA: CWB chief says no ships diverted to US ports now.
newsitem.headline: CWB chief says no ships diverted to US ports now.

text.p: No Asian vessels berthed in Vancouver have been diverted to United States ports to load U.S. spring wheat at this time but the Canadian Wheat Board has passed on wheat sales in the February-March delivery period, CWB chief commissioner Lorne Hehn told Reuters.

"I don't know that that rumour has any merit. We've had to pass up sales because we're not able to accomodate the February-March deliveries. We haven't deferred any (current) sales yet because of the late loadings," Hehn said.
There were 12 Japanese ships waiting to load Canadian spring wheat on the Pacific Coast Friday while one Japanese ship loaded grain. A total of 38 vessels waited to load Feb 7, Hehn added.
The CWB has had to pay C$8,000-C$10,000 a day per vessel in demurrage fees since early January with the bill now exceeding C$15 million, Hehn said.
"We've got some vessels waiting more than 30 days," he said.
Heavy snow, the cold, and sporadic Prairie elevator grain deliveries were blamed by shippers for the delay.
Consequently, rumours surfaced that Asian buyers were deferring Canadian wheat purchases and diverting ships to Portland, Ore., for immediately loading of U.S. spring wheat.
"Japan's weekly tender comes out tomorrow (Wednesday) and I haven't seen anything to suggest they're buying U.S. wheat because of this," Hehn added.
Officials at Canadian National Railway Co and Canadian Pacific unit CP Rail System were not immediately available for comment.
Hehn last week asked Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale to assist in expediting grain shipments.
Goodale planned to speak with the CWB and shippers this week, Goodale spokesman Vern Greenshields said.
